extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent attorneys, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of U.S. patentability bars, disclosure requirements (35 U.S.C. §112), claim-drafting/definiteness principles, and standards for patent infringement (direct, contributory, and induced), including claim construction and literal/equivalent infringement doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar (§102(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Events (sales, offers for sale, solicitations) more than one year prior to the U.S. application date can bar patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sale does not have to be public (a sale under a secrecy agreement can raise a §102(b) on-sale bar). Offers for sale and solicitation for orders may also give rise to the on-sale bar. The product offered need not be on hand and ready for delivery, but when the product does not exist the application of the bar is unclear. Sales made primarily for bona fide experimental purposes do not raise a §102(b) on-sale bar. To determine whether an invention was on sale, consider the totality of the circumstances and the policies underlying the bar: (1) preventing extension of the patent period, (2) preventing removal of inventions from the public domain which the public reasonably believes are freely available, (3) encouraging prompt disclosure, and (4) allowing reasonable time after sales to determine economic value. §102(b) creates a one-year risk-free period during which inventor may perfect and market invention; acts within that year do not give rise to the bar, but waiting more than a year risks §102(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment (§102(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor loses the right to obtain a patent if he or she abandons the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 102(c)’s abandonment is distinct from §102(g). For §102(c) to apply, the inventor must intend to abandon the invention; intent can be express or implied from a long and unexcused delay in filing. Decisions under §102(c) are rare. Abandoning a patent application (filing abandonment) does not by itself constitute §102(c) abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing/patenting bar (§102(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor loses the right to a U.S. patent if the inventor filed for a foreign patent or an inventor’s certificate more than 12 months before the U.S. filing date and the invention was patented or was the subject of an inventor’s certificate prior to the U.S. filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within §102(d) an invention is ‘patented’ when it confers legal rights; unlike §102(a), the foreign patent need not be publicly available. The provision encourages prompt U.S. filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (§112, ¶1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it, in full, clear, concise, and exact terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must describe the invention sought to be patented; because claims are part of the specification, what is described in the original claims is necessarily described in the original specification. Problems arise when claims are changed relying on the original specification: the issue is whether the originally filed specification describes what is in the new claims. It is not necessary to describe word-for-word what is in the new claims; it need only convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor invented what is in the new claims. Determination is case-by-case with little precedential value for fact-specific decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (§112, ¶1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable any person skilled in the pertinent art to make and carry out the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three important enablement issues: (1) the knowledge of the hypothetical person skilled in the art (presumed to know what is generally and reasonably available to the U.S. public — less than the §103 hypothetical who knows all relevant prior art), (2) the point in time when the specification must be enabling (it must be enabling when filed; exception exists when inventor indicates ability/willingness to make an indescribable trade secret available at patent grant), and (3) what constitutes 'undue experimentation' (some experimentation is allowed — e.g., adjusting parameters — but not experimentation that is unreasonable under the circumstances, such as requiring years of programming with no supplied program). Case citations: In re Buchner, White Consol., In re Howarth, Hybritech, In re Wands, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement-to-use (use requirement under §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable one skilled in the pertinent art to use the invention (distinct from utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention that does not work will not satisfy this requirement. Enabling use may require specific examples (e.g., for a compound that kills fungi, at least one example applying a particular amount to a particular fungus). Satisfying utility does not necessarily satisfy this enable-to-use requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (§112, ¶1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must disclose the best mode of carrying out the claimed invention contemplated by the inventor at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor knows or believes a particular mode (e.g., running at 7 degrees F) is best, that mode must be disclosed. §112 ¶1 is satisfied if the inventor believed the disclosed mode was the best at filing, even if it was not actually the best in reality. To prove violation, show the applicant knew of and concealed a better mode than disclosed. Disclosure of particular manufacturing procedures is not necessarily required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of adding new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If the initially filed specification does not fulfill §112 ¶1 requirements, adding new matter is required to cure deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding new matter causes the inventor to lose the original filing date, which may cause loss of patent rights because of statutory time bars (e.g., §102(b)). Therefore, when sufficiency of disclosure is challenged, inventors try to show the original specification met the four §112 ¶1 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be as definite as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the metes and bounds of the patent's exclusionary power and must be presented as definite as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a claim is sufficiently definite is determined in light of the relevant prior art and the particular application. A claim is not necessarily indefinite because it defines the invention by function or by product-by-process rather than by structure. See cases like Amgen v. Chugai and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of patent infringement proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement, determine whether someone (1) without authority (2) makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, or imports (3) the patented invention (4) within the United States/territories (5) during the term of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory framing (35 U.S.C. §271(a) and related provisions) guides infringement inquiries; other persons may also be liable under different theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization / Without authority (exhaustion and licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorization to make/use/sell normally comes from the patent owner (license); a licensee acting within scope does not infringe; an authorized sale can create an implied license (exhaustion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: geographical licenses — a license to sell east of Mississippi prevents infringement there but not west. Once there has been an authorized sale of the patented invention, buyer is impliedly authorized to repair, use, and resell the purchased item. The authorized sale of a nonpatented item used to practice a patented invention does not by itself create an implied license unless circumstances plainly indicate a license should be implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of 'makes', 'uses', 'sells', 'offers to sell', 'imports'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Makes' means creating an operable assembly of the patented invention; 'uses' means other than mere possession or experimental use; 'sells' means making a sale (not merely offering to sell); 'offers to sell' and 'imports' added by GATT-implementing legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms have distinct legal meanings; 'uses' excludes experimental and mere possession; an offer to sell (pre-GATT) could give rise to on-sale bar but the statute distinguishes offer vs sale for infringement at times. GATT changes expanded infringement to include offers to sell and imports for some patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who make, use, or sell the patented invention are direct infringers; corporate officers can be personally liable only if corporate veil is pierced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct infringers are not the only liable parties; courts recognize aiding and abetting theories (contributory and induced infringement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement (§271(c)) — four statutory elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A seller may be liable as a contributory infringer if: (1) the seller sells a component of a patented machine/manufacture/combination/composition, or material/apparatus for use in practicing a patented process; (2) the item sold constitutes a material part of the invention; (3) the seller knows the item is especially made or adapted for use in an infringement of a patent; and (4) the item sold is not a staple article or commodity of commerce suitable for substantial noninfringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The buyer must be a direct infringer. Liability requires seller's knowledge (a notice letter from the patent owner alleging infringement satisfies knowledge). If the item sold is suitable for substantial noninfringing uses (a 'staple'), contributory liability normally does not arise (e.g., gold sold generally is not contributory infringement even if buyer uses gold in infringing way).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced infringement (§271(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability for actively inducing infringement is imposed on one who actively induces another to infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inducement requires direct infringement by someone other than the inducer and requires specific, knowing intent to induce infringement. A person who sells a component and instructs the buyer how to practice a patented invention can be liable for inducing infringement even if not liable under contributory infringement. Corporate officers can be held liable for actively inducing their corporation's direct infringement regardless of veil-piercing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-patent rights and products made by patented processes (§271(g) and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patented invention is a process, the patent owner may exclude others from using, selling, or importing products made by the patented process throughout the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product is not deemed made by the patented process if materially changed by subsequent processes or if it becomes a trivial/nonessential component of another product. A rebuttable presumption that a product was made by the patented process arises if court finds substantial likelihood that product was so made and patent owner made a reasonable effort to determine the actual process used. There are statutory limitations on damages and detailed conditions; GATT-implementing legislation expanded rights to include offers to sell or importing products made by the patented process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction (meaning of claim terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining what the words in a claim mean (claim construction) is a question of law for the court; determining whether the construed claim covers the accused product/process is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to the patent's specification (written description, drawings, other claims), the prosecution history (file wrapper), and possibly extrinsic evidence (expert testimony). Words may mean their ordinary meaning to one skilled in the art or, if the inventor acts as his/her own lexicographer, a different meaning. Extrinsic evidence may help construe claim language but is not used to vary claim terms. Means-plus-function language is construed to include only structure, material, or acts (and their equivalents) described in the specification as performing the claimed function (35 U.S.C. §112 ¶6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is literally infringed if each properly construed claim element reads on the accused product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For means-plus-function elements, literal infringement occurs only when the accused product/process (a) employs means identical to those disclosed in the specification to perform the identical function, or (b) employs a means that is the structural equivalent of the means disclosed to perform the identical function. Example: a claim reciting a solid rod attaching blades would not literally read on a fan with a hollow rod because the solid-rod element is absent. Product-by-process claims read on products made by the identical process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: If one or more claim elements are not literally present but are found to be equivalent to claimed elements, infringement may be found under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining equivalence under the doctrine of equivalents differs from equivalence in means-plus-function analysis. There are limitations on the doctrine of equivalents (discussed elsewhere in the text), and a judicially created reverse doctrine of equivalents can sometimes limit infringement findings.
